transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-01-18 14:30 UTC | Duration 52 minutes | Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE); Priya Shah (Redwood SE); Alex Rivera (NimbleOps CTO); Samir Patel (Platform); Lena Wu (ML)

Summary: Quick discovery to validate integration approach. NimbleOps runs an internal gateway/proxy, evaluating hosted vs dedicated Redwood options. Main concerns: rate limits, token accounting, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter compatibility, observability hooks and tracing, VPC constraints, and enterprise security (KMS/SSO).

Topics: integration patterns, SDK + LangChain adapters, proxy vs sidecar, token rate quotas, streaming traces, KV/prefix cache behavior, private deployment constraints.

Action items (captured verbally): see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Jordan from Redwood. Quick intros?
[00:06] Alex Rivera: Alex here, CTO at NimbleOps, we run a customer-facing AI inference routing layer, want to make sure integration doesn't blow up our quotas.
[00:11] Samir Patel: Samir, platform eng, I own the gateway and rate limiting.
[00:16] Lena Wu: Lena, ML eng, I handle the embed and retrieval stack; we use LlamaIndex a lot.
[00:22] Priya Shah: Hi, Priya SE — I'll walk through observability and the sandbox tests.

[00:35] Jordan Kim: Great. Quick agenda: SDKs and adapter story for LangChain / LlamaIndex, how a proxy or gateway sits in front of Redwood, how rate limits and quotas map to our billing and per-token accounting, and what hooks you get for tracing and metrics.
[00:50] Alex Rivera: Sound good. Our main constraint is that we need per-customer rate shaping and cost attribution. We also have a strict VPC egress policy so hosted calls have to go through a corporate NAT.
[01:05] Priya Shah: Noted. We do have private deployment (VPC/on-prem) options if egress is a blocker, but often customers use our hosted API with VPC peering or a proxy. You mentioned LlamaIndex — can you tell us how you're calling models today?
[01:20] Lena Wu: Right now LlamaIndex wraps local models and some hosted endpoints. We call via a small connector that sends chat completions and embeddings. We'll need to swap endpoints easily and preserve cache keys, KV context, that sort of thing.
[01:36] Samir Patel: Another thing: we want to maintain our own rate limiter and apply backpressure before hitting Redwood. Do you have a recommended pattern — upstream proxy or Redwood-side quotas?
[01:50] Jordan Kim: Two patterns we see: 1) Edge-first: you keep your gateway rate limiting and map downstream to Redwood, implement token budgeting in the gateway to avoid spikes. 2) Redwood-side quotas: set per-api-key quotas (hosted) or per-tenant policies (dedicated/private). Often customers do both — gateway for real-time shaping, Redwood quotas for protection and billing.
[02:10] Alex Rivera: How deterministic is token accounting? We have complex prompt templating so we need predictable spend so finance can forecast.
[02:21] Priya Shah: Our accounting is token-based but there are nuances: streaming vs non-streaming can affect counting, system tokens and function call metadata sometimes get included or excluded depending on SDK call shape. We'll share a doc that explains token boundaries. Generally 95% stable but some edge cases.
[02:38] Lena Wu: That token doc would be great. Also, we use LangChain chains — is there a Redwood SDK connector for LangChain or LlamaIndex?
[02:46] Jordan Kim: We have official SDKs with example adapters for LangChain. LlamaIndex integrations are community-first but our SDK can be used to implement a connector; we also provide examples for the request middlewares to inject API key rotation, retry logic, and streaming handlers. Priya can share a sample repo.
[03:05] Priya Shah: I'll drop the LangChain connector link. Note: when using LangChain streaming callbacks, you want to register our streaming handler to keep latency low and avoid double buffering.
[03:18] Samir Patel: About proxies: we run an Envoy-based gateway. Will Redwood accept a high QPS connection from a single host or do you recommend multiplexing across IPs?
[03:29] Jordan Kim: For Hosted, we do enforce rate limits per API key and per-account; a single host making all requests is fine but you may see throttling if you hit the per-second quota. For Dedicated you can provision higher throughput and pin capacity; Private gives you full control. If you want consistent 1k rps you'll probably want Dedicated.
[03:46] Samir Patel: How about burst capacity and graceful degradation? If we hit a spike, will Redwood queue requests or return 429s?
[03:54] Priya Shah: We return 429s on soft limits; we also have throttling headers that indicate Retry-After and quota windows. For Dedicated, you can enable burst buffers and automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant that we call a 'compat' route — the runtime can route to a smaller quantized model to preserve latency.
[04:12] Alex Rivera: Interesting, we might use the compat route. On observability — what signals do we get out-of-box?
[04:20] Jordan Kim: OOB you'll get per-request latency, token counts, model id, region, and status codes in the Console. We emit traces that you can link into jaeger/zipkin via our tracing hook, and push metrics to Prometheus pushgateway or via DataDog exporter.
[04:36] Lena Wu: Do you provide context-level tracing to tie an embedding+chat sequence together? Our pipeline makes multiple calls per user convo and we need to stitch them.
[04:45] Priya Shah: Yes — we surface a request trace_id you can pass in X-Redwood-Trace header. If you pass the same trace_id across calls we aggregate them in the Console trace view. There are some limits on retention for hosted plans. For Dedicated/Private you can configure longer retention windows.
[05:01] Samir Patel: About SSO and audit logs — we require SAML for admin console and audit logs to be forwarded to our SIEM.
[05:10] Jordan Kim: SSO (SAML/SCIM) is supported for Dedicated and Private customers; hosted plans have SSO options for enterprise tiers. Audit logs can be exported to S3 or a syslog endpoint; Private can push directly into your SIEM via VPN.
[05:22] Alex Rivera: KMS and encryption at rest? We need to ensure embeddings stored for caching are customer-keyed.
[05:29] Priya Shah: For Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM; for Dedicated you can bring your own key in some cases. Hosted supports customer-managed keys for enterprise with extra controls. We'll share the KMS guide.
[05:42] Lena Wu: On caching — how does prefix / KV cache behave with LLM state? If we serve cached KV for context tokens, do we still pay for those tokens upstream?
[05:53] Jordan Kim: Good question. We do prefix caching where common prefixes are cached and not re-sent to the model. Billing is on tokens processed by the runtime; if the prefix is served from cache and not re-tokenized to the model, you do not pay for those tokens in most configurations. But you'll still see them in trace context for debugging. There are edge cases with function call payloads where tokens are reconstituted.
[06:15] Samir Patel: We'll need config knobs: cache TTL, eviction policy, and ability to purge keys per-tenant.
[06:22] Priya Shah: Those exist in Dedicated/Private; hosted has a managed cache with per-namespace TTLs but not full purge by default — you can request a purge via support for enterprise customers.
[06:35] Alex Rivera: For the sandbox benchmark — we want to simulate 10k requests/day with spikes to 300 rps for 2 minutes. Can you replicate that load?
[06:44] Priya Shah: Yes. We'll provision a sandbox with the smallest dedicated pool and run the workload. We'll also instrument traces and share a spreadsheet with latency percentiles and cost per 1000 tokens.
[06:57] Lena Wu: About SDK specifics — what languages and is there a go SDK? Our gateway is go-based.
[07:04] Jordan Kim: Official SDKs: Python, Node, Go, and Java. Go SDK supports both sync and streaming APIs. There's a middleware pattern for automatic retry, idempotency keys, and request batching.
[07:16] Samir Patel: Batching — can we aggregate small requests server-side or do you recommend client-side batching? We're worried about tail latency.
[07:25] Priya Shah: Redwood runtime does continuous batching for tokens on the serving side to optimize throughput; client-side batching helps reduce per-request overhead but can add latency. We recommend client-side micro-batching for small requests, combined with our server-side batching. We'll share our best-practice tuning doc.
[07:40] Alex Rivera: Any pitfalls with LangChain chains and function-calling patterns? We use function calls extensively.
[07:48] Jordan Kim: Function calls change token patterns and callbacks; they often increase roundtrips. Watch system tokens and ensure your callback handlers are idempotent. LangChain's built-in retriers sometimes double-invoke if you don't set an idempotency key — our SDK supports that header.
[08:05] Lena Wu: For LlamaIndex, we rely on local index lookups and then call model. Will Redwood allow us to pin a model version so behavior remains consistent?
[08:14] Priya Shah: Yes, on all deployment modes you can pin model versions. For Hosted there is a model catalog and you can set model_version in the request; Dedicated and Private allow you to bring quantized variants and pin to a commit.
[08:28] Samir Patel: Ok, talk to me about observability hooks: metrics, sampling rate, and custom spans.
[08:36] Jordan Kim: We emit OpenTelemetry spans. You can set sampling rate per-API-key and add custom attributes. For high-volume customers we suggest sampling at 1% and enabling trace_id propagation for key sessions. We also send application metrics (requests/sec, tokens/sec, cache hit rate) to Prometheus or Datadog.
[08:52] Alex Rivera: If we sample, will we lose the ability to debug incidents?
[08:56] Priya Shah: You can do adaptive sampling — keep 100% traces for errors and 1% for normal traffic. Dedicated customers can keep more retention. We can also configure per-user or per-tenant trace retention for compliance windows.
[09:12] Samir Patel: Are there rate-limit headers so our proxy can surface remaining quota back to users?
[09:18] Jordan Kim: Yes — X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After, plus a header for token-balance if you use token-bucket billing. For enterprise we can add custom headers.
[09:29] Lena Wu: On error modes, if Redwood falls back to a compat route, do you surface that in metrics? We need to detect when model downgraded for quality alerts.
[09:38] Priya Shah: The Console has a route-level metric for fallback events; we also emit a header X-Redwood-Fallback: true. You can wire that into your alerts.
[09:48] Alex Rivera: Our legal team cares about data residency. Can hosted guarantee EU-only data stays in EU?
[09:55] Jordan Kim: We have region pinning for hosted — you can choose models served from eu-west-1 and restrict data residency. For stricter needs, Dedicated or Private recommended.
[10:05] Samir Patel: One operational question: if we onboard to Dedicated, what's the usual lead time?
[10:11] Priya Shah: Typical is 4-8 weeks depending on capacity and network setup. Private on-prem is longer. We'll need network peering, VPN and security review.
[10:20] Alex Rivera: Any live migration plan if we start hosted and want dedicated in 3 months?
[10:25] Jordan Kim: Yes — we support canary rollouts and model/version pinning. You can start hosted, then move traffic gradually to Dedicated by switching route policy via the Console or API.
[10:36] Samir Patel: About cost — can you provide cost-per-embed and per-token examples for our traffic shape?
[10:42] Priya Shah: We'll run the sandbox and give cost projections. You'll get a cost breakdown: serving tokens, inference GPU minutes for dedicated, and cache savings.
[10:52] Lena Wu: Ok, last technical: healthchecks and circuit breakers. If Redwood has a transient error, do you provide retry-after windows or suggest client patterns?
[11:02] Jordan Kim: We emit Retry-After and 429s. Our SDKs have built-in exponential backoff and jitter. For mission-critical flows we recommend circuit breaker with a short window and fallback to a cached response or read-only variant.
[11:16] Alex Rivera: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[11:19] Jordan Kim: Recap: Jordan to share LangChain connector and observability runbook; Priya to provision sandbox and configure tracing/reporting; Samir to share traffic profiles and sample payloads; NimbleOps to confirm timeline for a 3-week pilot.
[11:33] Samir Patel: We'll send payloads by Friday. Pilot timeline tentatively two weeks after sandbox ready.
[11:38] Lena Wu: Also please include notes on token accounting edge cases — function call tokens and streaming differences.
[11:44] Priya Shah: Will do. Any final questions?
[11:48] Alex Rivera: No, thanks. Good session.

End of transcript.
